summaries.gardner: Wells Fargo fits Rule Breaker investing poorly: it is a 174-year-old incumbent in mature US banking, not the leader of an emerging industry, and its brand is still tied to the 2016 fake-accounts scandal. Revenue grew only from $74.4B in 2022 to $83.7B in 2025, and the stock rose just 2.5% over the past 52 weeks.
summaries.buffett: Wells Fargo was once one of Berkshire Hathaway's biggest holdings, but Buffett sold out by 2022 after the sales-practices scandal damaged his trust in management. Today it is understandable, consistently profitable and modestly priced (about 12.9 times 2025 EPS of $6.26 and 1.5 times book), but returns (14.6% ROTCE in 2025) depend on leverage and the brand moat is weaker than it was.
summaries.munger: Munger valued simple businesses with durable advantages run by trustworthy people, and Wells Fargo's long incentive-driven misconduct is a textbook case of the incentive-caused bias he warned about. The franchise's cheap deposits remain valuable and Charlie Scharf has repaired controls, but inverting the problem shows real failure routes: credit losses, rate pressure and renewed regulatory trouble.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class Wells Fargo as a stalwart turned turnaround: the Fed lifted its asset cap in June 2025 and diluted EPS rose 17% in 2025 and 18% in the first nine months of 2026. With a trailing P/E near 11-13 against mid-teens EPS growth and the share count down from 4,134 million in 2020 to about 3,052 million, it passes his P/E-to-growth test, though the story is not a hidden one.
summaries.fisher: Wells Fargo scores weakly on Fisher's growth-focused points: revenue has barely grown since 2021, it is not known for new products or R&D, and sales-culture abuses rather than sales skill defined its recent history. Management depth and cost control have improved under Scharf, but it is not the long-term compounding grower Fisher sought.
summaries.graham: Wells Fargo passes several of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it is large, has been profitable every year for at least ten years, has paid dividends for decades, grew EPS from $4.15 in 2015 to $6.26 in 2025, and P/E times P/B is about 20. It falls short on financial strength in Graham's industrial sense, since like all banks it carries liabilities of about 11.7 times equity.
summaries.thiel: Wells Fargo does not fit Thiel's Zero to One model: it sells commodity banking products with no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and competes in a crowded oligopoly with JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citigroup. Its distribution (branches and a large deposit base) is strong, but it is not a monopoly built on a secret.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price and management that is 'fit' on costs; Wells Fargo shows the cost discipline (efficiency ratio 63% in Q3 2026, headcount falling) and a low multiple (forward P/E about 10.4). However, mid-single-digit revenue growth and no clear role in the AI platform shift make it a weak fit for his growth-oriented approach.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades on liquidity, rates and catalysts, and Wells Fargo is a leveraged play on the US economy and bank deregulation after the 2025 asset-cap removal. Falling rates have squeezed its net interest margin (2.43% in Q3 2026 vs 2.61%), so the macro set-up is mixed rather than strongly favourable.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith's Fundsmith avoids banks because their returns depend on leverage and they have little control over their own fate in a downturn. Wells Fargo's 12.4% ROE in 2025, high leverage and rate sensitivity put it outside his 'good company' criteria despite a reasonable valuation.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula excludes banks and other financial companies because return on capital and earnings yield are not meaningful for leveraged balance sheets. On rough measures Wells Fargo is cheap (forward P/E about 10.4) but its returns on capital are ordinary once leverage is considered.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a high-return business, skilled and honest management, and abundant reinvestment opportunities. Wells Fargo now has competent management and room to grow after the asset cap, but its 14.6% ROTCE relies on leverage and its history of misconduct weakens the integrity leg.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary distress bought at deep discounts; Wells Fargo was such a case during the asset-cap years, but at 1.8 times tangible book and with the cap already lifted in June 2025, the distress and much of the discount are gone. Downside risk is moderate rather than minimal given bank leverage.
summaries.wood: Wells Fargo is the kind of incumbent ARK expects digital wallets, fintechs and blockchain to disrupt, not an innovation platform leader. Nothing in its business fits ARK's disruptive-innovation themes.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and limited outside risks; Wells Fargo is simple to describe and now improving returns, but its earnings depend on rates, credit and regulators. It fits his turnaround style more than his core quality criteria.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep sought companies that share scale economies with customers and grow stronger over decades; Wells Fargo keeps cost savings mainly for shareholders through buybacks and has been shrinking headcount rather than lowering prices. Its position in 10-20 years looks similar to today rather than clearly stronger.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking huge new markets with a technology shift, which Wells Fargo is not. It is a mature, regulated incumbent serving an existing market.
summaries.nash: Wells Fargo fails most of Nash's screens: revenue growth is single-digit, it carries more borrowings ($221.0B) than cash ($181.1B) and, like all banks, fails his lending-style balance-sheet tests. It scores well on profitability, low short interest, consistent EPS beats and a cheap valuation (PEG about 0.75), but does not sell into a secular growth trend.

momentum.evidence: The shares were up only 2.51% over the 52 weeks to October 14, 2026 ($80.90), and trade below their 50-day ($85.40) and 200-day ($84.27) moving averages.

g4.evidence: Charlie Scharf (ex-CEO of Visa and BNY Mellon) has a strong record, but Berkshire Hathaway sold out of Wells Fargo by 2022 and no prominent investor is now associated with the stock.

g6.evidence: At about 10.4 times forward earnings with a $97.90 average analyst target, the stock is generally seen as fairly or under-valued, not overvalued.

simple.evidence: It is a traditional US bank taking deposits, making loans and earning fees across four segments, understandable to a careful generalist.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year, but results slumped after the 2016 scandal (2020 net income only $3.4B) and revenue in 2025 ($83.7B) was still below 2015's $86.1B.

integrity.evidence: Governance has improved under Scharf and regulators lifted the asset cap in June 2025, but the bank's history of opening millions of fake accounts and repeated consent orders weighs on its record of candour.

b6.evidence: Management has avoided large acquisitions and sold non-core businesses (such as rail car leasing in Q1 2026), but is now expanding investment banking and trading, partly to catch up with peers.

roic.evidence: Returns are moderate and leverage-driven: ROE was 12.4% and ROTCE 14.6% in 2025, with liabilities about 11.7 times equity.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank; earnings ($21.3B in 2025) are largely returned through dividends and buybacks.

b10.evidence: Tangible book value per share rose only from $44.18 (Sep 2025) to $44.46 (Sep 2026) as most earnings went to buybacks, though the share count fell from 4,134 million diluted shares in 2020 to 3,052 million.

safety.evidence: At $80.90 the shares trade at about 1.8 times tangible book value of $44.46 and 12.9 times 2025 EPS, so there is no clear margin of safety against a conservative value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 10.4 and trailing P/E of 11.4 look reasonable for a bank growing EPS 18% in the first nine months of 2026 with 16.3% ROTCE.

mu5.evidence: A deep recession with heavy credit losses, a renewed regulatory crackdown or a deposit run are plausible failure routes for a leveraged bank, though its size and $1.5 trillion deposit base make collapse unlikely.

reinvest.evidence: With the asset cap lifted it can grow loans (average loans $1,033.4B in Q3 2026 vs $928.7B) at mid-teens returns on tangible equity, but growth is tied to the US economy.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart turnaround: the story is the post-asset-cap recovery, with diluted EPS up from $3.27 in 2022 to $6.26 in 2025.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 11.4-12.9 is below diluted EPS growth of 17% in 2025 and 18% in the first nine months of 2026.

runway.evidence: Revenue is expected to grow about 5% in 2026 to $87.9B; as a mature US-only bank its sales cannot grow substantially into new places.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 4,134.2 million in 2020 to 3,051.5 million in Q3 2026 through buybacks, but no open-market insider purchases were found.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the most heavily covered US stocks, with about 27 analysts and 78.8% institutional ownership.

fi2.evidence: It has launched new card products (Autograph, Active Cash) and is building out investment banking, but product development is not a core strength.

fi3.evidence: Wells Fargo does not report R&D; its technology spending is not disclosed in a way that allows judging results.

fi4.evidence: Its aggressive cross-selling culture led to the 2016 fake-accounts scandal, and it is not known for superior sales ability today.

longterm.evidence: Scharf spent years rebuilding risk controls before growth, a long-term choice, but heavy buybacks that cut CET1 to 10.0% favour near-term per-share returns.

gr1.evidence: It is one of the four largest US banks, with about $2.25 trillion of assets and a market value of about $243B.

ni10.evidence: Wells Fargo reported a profit in every year from 2016 to 2025, including $3.4B in the pandemic year 2020.

gr4.evidence: Wells Fargo has paid a common dividend every year for decades, including through 2009 and 2020 when it cut the payout but did not suspend it; the quarterly dividend is now $0.50.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.15 in 2015 to $6.26 in 2025, an increase of about 51%.

gr6.evidence: At $80.90 the price is about 14.7 times average diluted EPS of the last three years ($4.83, $5.37, $6.26).

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 12.9 times price/book of about 1.53 gives roughly 20, under 22.5.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; its banking products are comparable to JPMorgan's and Bank of America's.

timing.evidence: Removal of the asset cap in June 2025 and a lighter regulatory stance give it room to grow now, but falling rates are squeezing its net interest margin.

th3.evidence: Wells Fargo did not start with a dominant share of a small niche; it grew through mergers (notably Norwest in 1998 and Wachovia in 2008) into a broad national bank.

team.evidence: Charlie Scharf and his team are seasoned and have delivered the regulatory turnaround, but are not seen as a world-class founder-led team.

th5.evidence: It has one of the largest US branch, ATM and digital distribution networks, serving tens of millions of customers.

durable.evidence: Large US banks have proven durable, but fintechs, private credit and payments innovation could erode parts of its franchise over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: It pursues the same banking opportunities as its large peers, without a unique insight others miss.

trend.evidence: It is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud; it is a user of these technologies like every other bank.

dr1.evidence: Diluted EPS rose 13% year on year to $1.87 in Q3 2026, but revenue of $21.87B missed the roughly $22.3B consensus, so estimates are not clearly rising.

dr2.evidence: Balance-sheet growth after the asset cap and ongoing efficiency gains could lift returns further, but this recovery story is already widely known.

dr4.evidence: Deregulation and a growing economy help, but lower rates cut its net interest margin to 2.43% in Q3 2026 from 2.61% a year earlier.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include continued buybacks ($2.5B in Q3 2026), loan growth now that the asset cap is gone, and potential easing of bank capital rules.

dr7.evidence: As a leveraged, rate- and credit-sensitive bank growing revenue in single digits, it is unlikely to warrant a large concentrated position under Druckenmiller's approach.

gm.evidence: Banks do not report gross margin; its net interest margin was 2.43% in Q3 2026, typical for a large US bank.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank; its earnings yield is about 8% (2025 EPS $6.26 on an $80.90 price).

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not meaningful for a bank, whose deposits and borrowings are operating items.

pa2.evidence: The temporary setback (the 2018-2025 Fed asset cap) has already been fixed, so the discount from it has largely closed.

pa4.evidence: Its size, $177.9B of equity and a 10.0% CET1 ratio make permanent loss unlikely, but bank leverage of about 11.7 times equity means a severe crisis could hurt shareholders.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its product costs do not fall rapidly with volume in a way that opens large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms; it is a traditional bank.

wo4.evidence: Its US banking market will not be many times larger in five years; consensus expects revenue growth around 5-6% a year.

ac3.evidence: Its earnings depend heavily on interest rates (net interest income $47.5B in 2025) and the credit cycle.

ns1.evidence: It uses scale savings mainly to raise returns and buy back shares (headcount cut to 205,198 at end-2025) rather than lowering prices for customers.

ns4.evidence: It should be in a better position than during the asset-cap years, but not clearly stronger relative to JPMorgan or fintech rivals in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: Safe deposits, payments and credit are essential needs, but they are already well served by many banks.

tn1.evidence: It is a traditional bank, not a company built to serve a secular trend like AI or energy.

tn2.evidence: The market sees it as a recovering large US bank, which is what it is becoming.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company outside the avoid zones (small caps, Chinese firms, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses, startups).

tn4.evidence: It is profitable ($21.3B net income in 2025) and revenue rose in 2023 and 2025, but it has more borrowings ($221.0B) than cash ($181.1B) and revenue dipped in 2024; bank leverage is a structural reason for the miss.

tn5.evidence: Borrowings exceeded cash and due from banks plus interest-earning deposits in recent quarters (e.g. $221.0B vs $181.1B at September 30, 2026), and free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 1.7% in 2025 and is expected to grow about 5% in 2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 2-5% plus an unmeasurable bank free-cash-flow margin does not reach 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue rose 1.7% to $83.7B while noninterest expense rose 0.4% to $54.8B.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: borrowings exceed cash and revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: The asset cap and most consent orders are gone, but as a systemically important bank with a misconduct history it remains under close regulatory scrutiny.

tn11.evidence: It provides deposit accounts, loans and investment services that help US households and businesses manage money and borrow, charging interest spreads and fees, chosen mainly for its national branch network and convenience.

tn13.evidence: Total about 60 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0 (not verified as ahead), moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2022 and 2024, borrowings exceeded cash, and free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank.

tn15.evidence: Like all banks it fails these tests, with total liabilities about 11.7 times equity at September 30, 2026.

tn18.evidence: Scharf has executed well since October 2019 (ROTCE up to 16.3%), but has been CEO under 10 years, is not the founder and no open-market share purchases were found.

tn20.evidence: Wells Fargo beat consensus EPS in each of the last six reported quarters through Q3 2026, though revenue missed in Q3 2026.

tn21.evidence: There is no current accounting issue or co-CEO structure, but the 2016 fake-accounts fraud and years of consent orders are a historical red flag.

tn24.evidence: At about 11-13 times earnings the price implies low single-digit growth, below the 17-18% EPS growth it delivered in 2025 and 2026 year to date.

tn25.evidence: A free-cash-flow DCF is not meaningful for a bank, whose cash flows are dominated by deposit and loan movements.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 10.4 with a PEG of about 0.75 looks attractive for a large US bank growing EPS in the mid-teens.
